rhythmSection.intro: Pool care is less about effort and more about cadence. Tap a timeframe to see exactly what needs to happen — whether you do it yourself or hand it to us.

rhythm.label: Weekly
rhythm.title: The Weekly Reset
rhythm.description: Ninety percent of clear water comes from this short list. Skip two weeks in July and you'll spend a weekend fixing it.

tasks.title: Skim the surface
tasks.description: Net out leaves and bugs before they sink and start feeding algae.

tasks.title: Empty both baskets
tasks.description: Skimmer and pump baskets choke water flow long before the filter does.

tasks.title: Brush walls and steps
tasks.description: A soft nylon brush lifts the invisible film on the gelcoat, including the tanning ledge.

tasks.title: Vacuum the floor
tasks.description: Fine silt settles in the deep end and dulls the water even when chemistry is perfect.

tasks.title: Test chlorine and pH
tasks.description: Two strips, thirty seconds. Adjust while it's a small correction instead of a rescue.

tasks.title: Check the water level
tasks.description: Mid-skimmer is the target — too low and the pump starves and can run dry.

rhythm.label: Monthly
rhythm.title: The Deeper Check
rhythm.description: Monthly work is where you catch slow drifts — the ones that only show up as cloudy water three weeks later.

tasks.title: Full chemistry panel
tasks.description: Total alkalinity, cyanuric acid and calcium hardness, not just chlorine and pH.

tasks.title: Clean the filter
tasks.description: Rinse cartridges or backwash sand/DE once pressure climbs 8–10 psi above clean.

tasks.title: Inspect the equipment pad
tasks.description: Look for weeping unions, a tired pump lid o-ring, and unusual pump noise.

tasks.title: Detail the waterline
tasks.description: Sunscreen and body oils collect in a band at the surface — wipe it before it sets.

tasks.title: Check the salt cell
tasks.description: On salt systems, inspect the cell for scale and verify salinity sits at 3,000–3,500 ppm.

tasks.title: Scan for early stains
tasks.description: Catch metal or organic staining while it still rinses off with a brush.

rhythm.label: Seasonal
rhythm.title: Opening and Closing
rhythm.description: Ohio gives you two hinge points a year. Get these right and the season in between is quiet.

tasks.title: Spring opening
tasks.description: Pull the cover, refill to level, restart circulation and rebalance from scratch.

tasks.title: Deep clean the shell
tasks.description: Full brush, vacuum and waterline detail before the water gets warm enough for algae.

tasks.title: Strip the filter
tasks.description: A full teardown clean — or new cartridges — beats a season of weak filtration.

tasks.title: Service the cover
tasks.description: Test the auto cover mechanism, clean the fabric, and check tracks and ropes.

tasks.title: Fall winterization
tasks.description: Blow out the lines, drain the equipment and seal the pool for the freeze.

tasks.title: Heater check
tasks.description: Verify the heater before the first cold night, not after it.

rhythm.label: Annual
rhythm.title: The Yearly Once-Over
rhythm.description: One thorough look each year is what turns a $200 part into a repair you never had.

tasks.title: Professional inspection
tasks.description: Shell, coping, skimmer, plumbing and bonding reviewed end to end.

tasks.title: Replace filter media
tasks.description: Cartridges wear out after roughly 2–3 seasons; sand runs 5–7 years.

tasks.title: Pump and heater service
tasks.description: Seals, bearings, gaskets and pressure switches checked and replaced as needed.

tasks.title: Gelcoat assessment
tasks.description: We look for fading, chalking or crazing and tell you what caused it.

tasks.title: Electrical and automation
tasks.description: Bonding, GFCI protection, timers and app control verified and updated.

tasks.title: Water refresh plan
tasks.description: If stabilizer or hardness has climbed too far, we plan a partial exchange safely.

chemistrySection.intro: Almost every water problem is one of these six readings drifting out of range. Print this, tape it inside the equipment shed, and test twice a week in peak season.
chemistrySection.note: Ranges are general guidance for San Juan fiberglass pools. Salt, heated and automated systems may need tighter targets — we set yours on the first visit.

chemistry.name: pH
chemistry.why: Below 7.2 the water turns aggressive on gelcoat and metal parts. Above 7.8 chlorine goes lazy and scale forms.

chemistry.name: Free Chlorine
chemistry.why: Steady sanitizer beats heavy shocking. Letting it hit zero for a day is how algae gets its opening.

chemistry.name: Total Alkalinity
chemistry.why: This is pH's shock absorber. Too low and pH bounces daily; too high and it stubbornly climbs.

chemistry.name: Cyanuric Acid
chemistry.why: Sunscreen for your chlorine. Above 50 ppm it starts locking the sanitizer instead of protecting it.

chemistry.name: Calcium Hardness
chemistry.why: Fiberglass tolerates softer water than concrete, but very low calcium still leads to foaming and staining.

chemistry.name: Salt (salt systems)
chemistry.why: Below range the cell produces less chlorine and works harder; above range it corrodes hardware.

troubleshootSection.intro: Pick the symptom you're looking at. We'll tell you the usual cause, what to do first, and when it's time to call instead of guessing.

troubleshoot.label: Cloudy water
troubleshoot.cause: Filtration running too short, pH and alkalinity drifting high, or very fine debris the filter can't grab.
steps: Run the pump 10–12 hours a day until it clears
Clean the cartridges or backwash the filter
Bring pH back to 7.4–7.6 and alkalinity to 80–120 ppm
Brush the walls and floor, then vacuum what settles
Add a clarifier only after the filter is clean
troubleshoot.callUs: Still hazy after 48 hours of good filtration? The filter media or pump flow is the real problem — that's a service call.

troubleshoot.label: Green or algae
troubleshoot.cause: Chlorine hit zero, or cyanuric acid climbed high enough to lock the sanitizer you're adding.
steps: Brush every surface first — algae has to be broken loose to be killed
Test cyanuric acid before shocking; high CYA needs more shock, not less
Shock the pool and run circulation 24 hours straight
Clean the filter once, then again after the water turns cloudy grey
Hold free chlorine at 3 ppm for several days before relaxing
troubleshoot.callUs: A full green-to-clean recovery usually takes 3–5 days and several filter cleanings. We run it as a multi-visit program so you don't burn a week on it.

troubleshoot.label: Waterline ring
troubleshoot.cause: Sunscreen, body oils and airborne dust collecting in a band right at the water surface.
steps: Wipe the band with a soft cloth or sponge and a gelcoat-safe cleaner
Never use scouring pads, abrasive powders or magic-eraser style blocks
Drop a skimmer sock into the basket to catch oils continuously
Rinse the removed film out of the pool rather than pushing it under
troubleshoot.callUs: If the band has hardened into a rough calcium line, it needs a proper gelcoat-safe treatment — don't attack it with acid.

troubleshoot.label: Strong chlorine smell
troubleshoot.cause: Counterintuitive but common — that smell is chloramines, meaning spent chlorine, not too much of it.
steps: Test total chlorine and free chlorine; the gap between them is the problem
Shock the pool to break the chloramines apart
Run the pump overnight with the water feature on for aeration
Retest before anyone swims
troubleshoot.callUs: If the smell and eye irritation come back within days, sanitizer demand is outrunning your system — worth a look at the pad.

troubleshoot.label: Chlorine won't hold
troubleshoot.cause: Usually stabilizer out of range — either none at all, so sunlight burns it off, or far too much, which locks it up.
steps: Test cyanuric acid before adding anything else
At 0–20 ppm, add stabilizer so the sun stops eating your chlorine
Above 60 ppm, plan a partial water exchange to dilute it
Check for a heavy debris or organic load quietly consuming sanitizer
troubleshoot.callUs: Never drain a fiberglass pool to fix chemistry. A partial exchange has to be done carefully — call us and we'll handle the volume math.

troubleshoot.label: Stains or fading
troubleshoot.cause: Metals from fill water or a worn heater core, organic tannins from leaves, or chlorine held too high for too long.
steps: Hold a crushed vitamin C tablet on the stain — if it lightens, it's metal
For metal, add a sequestrant and stop the metal source
For organic, shock and brush the area, then vacuum
Keep free chlorine under 5 ppm going forward to protect the gelcoat color
troubleshoot.callUs: Never acid-wash or pressure-wash a fiberglass shell. Let us identify the stain first — the wrong fix is permanent.

rulesSection.intro: A fiberglass shell will outlive most of the equipment attached to it — as long as nobody cleans it like a concrete pool.

dos.heading: Do This
items: Use a soft nylon brush or a pool-rated non-abrasive pad
Keep free chlorine steady at 1–3 ppm instead of shocking hard
Pre-dissolve granular chemicals in a bucket before they go in
Run the pump long enough to turn the water over once a day
Empty the skimmer and pump baskets before they restrict flow
Keep the water level at mid-skimmer, especially in a dry August

donts.heading: Never Do This
items: No steel brushes, scouring pads or abrasive cleaning powders
No loose trichlor tabs sitting on the floor or parked in the skimmer
Don't drain the pool — a fiberglass shell can flex or float
Don't leave chlorine above 5 ppm for days; the color pays for it
No acid washing and no pressure washing the shell
Don't let leaves sit for weeks — tannins stain and they stain fast

serviceSection.paragraph: This is the list our crews work through on a cleaning trip. Not every line applies to every pool — a cartridge system never gets backwashed, a chlorine pool has no salt cell — so we run what your equipment calls for and tell you what we found.

images.alt: Fiberglass pool with clear blue water

checklist.title: 7-panel water test
checklist.description: A full panel, not a glance at a strip — chlorine, pH, alkalinity, stabilizer, hardness and the rest.

checklist.title: Test the salt level
checklist.description: On salt systems we read salinity, so the cell isn't working harder than it should or corroding hardware.

checklist.title: Check the chlorine feeder
checklist.description: The feeder is opened, inspected and set to the right rate for the season and the bather load.

checklist.title: Evaluate the salt cell
checklist.description: We inspect the cell for scale and clean it when it needs it, before output starts dropping.

checklist.title: Add chemicals, circulate and test
checklist.description: Doses go in, the water turns over, and we test again before we call it balanced.

checklist.title: Clean the baskets
checklist.description: Skimmer and pump baskets emptied, so flow isn't choked before the filter even sees the water.

checklist.title: Clean the cartridge filter
checklist.description: On cartridge systems the elements come out and get rinsed down properly.

checklist.title: Backwash sand filters
checklist.description: Sand systems get backwashed and the media checked for channeling, clumping and age.

checklist.title: Vacuum with E-vacs
checklist.description: A hose-powered vacuum with a debris bag — it lifts heavy leaves and silt without loading the filter.

checklist.title: Vacuum on pool suction
checklist.description: Vacuuming through the pool's own suction line for the fine settled silt a bag vac leaves behind.

faqSection.intro: The questions we get most often about keeping a fiberglass pool clear. If yours isn't here, just call — we'd rather answer it than have you guess.

faqs.question: How much does a pool cleaning cost?
faqs.answer: A one-time trip runs $250 to $400 depending on pool size, small to large. Regular service is two to three trips a month at $250 to $300 per trip, depending on the pool and the scope of the work. Condition matters as much as size — a pool that sat closed all season takes more than one that just needs its rhythm back. We confirm the number with you before any work starts.

faqs.question: How often does a fiberglass pool need to be cleaned?
faqs.answer: In season, plan on a weekly rhythm: skim, brush, vacuum, empty the baskets and test the water. A fiberglass shell needs less scrubbing than concrete because algae can't take hold in a non-porous gelcoat surface, but debris, oils and chemistry drift happen at the same rate in any pool. Most owners who hire us book two to three trips a month through the swim season.

faqs.question: Do fiberglass pools really need fewer chemicals?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the reason is physical rather than marketing. The gelcoat surface is smooth and non-porous, so there's no microscopic texture for algae to root into and no plaster leaching into the water and pushing pH up. Owners typically use noticeably less chlorine and acid than a comparable concrete pool. What doesn't change is the need to test — smaller corrections, just as often.

faqs.question: What kind of brush should I use on a fiberglass pool?
faqs.answer: A soft nylon-bristle brush, or a pool-rated non-abrasive pad for spot work. Never use a stainless or steel-bristle brush, a scouring pad, or an abrasive cleaning powder. Those are made for plaster and they leave permanent dull scratches in gelcoat. Same rule for the waterline: soft cloth and a gelcoat-safe cleaner only.

faqs.question: My pool turned green. How long does it take to fix?
faqs.answer: A typical green-to-clean recovery takes three to five days from the first treatment to swimmable water, and it usually needs several filter cleanings along the way. The sequence matters: brush first so the algae is broken loose, test stabilizer before dosing, shock, then keep circulation running around the clock. We run recovery as a structured multi-visit program rather than a single visit, because the filter work is what actually finishes the job.

faqs.question: Can I clean the pool myself and just call you when something's wrong?
faqs.answer: Absolutely, and plenty of our customers do exactly that. A one-time deep clean is a good reset if things got away from you, and we're happy to be the backup for algae blooms, equipment questions or a mid-season chemistry mess. We'll also show you how to read your own numbers so the calls get rarer.

faqs.question: Do you clean pools you didn't build?
faqs.answer: Yes. We service fiberglass, and we're happy to look at other pool types to tell you honestly whether we're the right crew for it. If your pool came from another builder, that's not a problem — we'll baseline the equipment and water on the first visit and go from there.

faqs.question: Can cleaning be bundled with opening and closing?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that's the combination most owners land on. Winterization assumes the pool is clean when we arrive, so bundling a cleaning visit with your closing avoids an extra fee and gives the pool a better winter. See our pool closing and opening page for what winterization covers, and mention the bundle when you book.
